title: Why Are Fetch Quests Boring? | Designing Meaningful Quests

scenes.title: Read the Actions Inside an Errand
lines: Bring back three items. It is a familiar request in games.
Some errands make you curious about the next destination,
while others just make you want to finish.
The difference may lie in what happens between the instruction and delivery.
We will compare travel and gathering in Skyrim with resource exploration in Subnautica,
then change conditions in an original delivery prototype.
We will examine three questions.
What choices happen along the way? What changes after delivery?
And does the return journey offer anything new?

scenes.title: Choices Along the Way
lines: First, look at the actions on the way, rather than only the destination.
When gathering materials in Subnautica, you inspect your surroundings
and use the remaining oxygen to decide whether to keep searching or surface.
This is not a quest assigned by a character,
but an example of a player seeking materials for their own needs.
A gathering goal can contain observation and decisions.
If following a marker leaves no action or route to choose,
extra travel time may add waiting rather than meaningful activity.
Write down the moments when players make decisions during your quest.
Check whether those choices actually exist between destinations.

scenes.title: Changes After Completion
lines: Next, examine what changes when the task is completed.
Here are travel and mining scenes from Skyrim.
This footage does not demonstrate the reward of a particular quest.
It illustrates the actions of travel and gathering.
The question for our own game is separate.
After delivering the items, does only the score increase?
Or does a route open, or someone behave differently?
A numerical reward can matter, but a visible consequence
may help players understand why the task mattered.
We will build that difference in a small delivery game.

scenes.title: Same Delivery, Different World State
lines: Both versions ask you to collect three logs along the same route and return.
Movement speed, item positions, and the score reward are identical.
In the first version, delivery raises the score and completes the request.
In the second, the same delivery repairs a broken bridge.
The places you can reach afterward actually change.
The bridge is more than decorative completion artwork.
A blocked collision area opens, allowing the character to cross.
This comparison demonstrates a change in the world state.
Whether the second version is more enjoyable still needs human playtesting.
A successful automated input trace is not an enjoyment rating.

scenes.title: Redesign the Return Journey
lines: Now examine the return journey.
You initially take a detour, but repairing the bridge opens a shorter route.
The same location now has a different role.
Another test adds a gate on the short route that requires an empty inventory.
You choose between returning quickly and carrying the item along the longer route.
The presence of a shortcut alone does not create a decision.
Players need to understand what they gain and give up.
You do not need an event during every moment of travel.
Quiet time can allow players to notice the surroundings or reflect.
First decide what purpose a repeated stretch should serve.

scenes.title: Test the Play with Three Questions
lines: When designing a quest, add three lines beneath its objective.
List choices on the way, changes after the task, and new information on return.
If all three are empty, before adding more requests,
introduce a small change in one stretch of the journey.
Ask players where they paused and which route they chose.
Check what they thought changed after completion.
Their understanding may differ from your design intent.
The number of items alone does not determine a good errand.
Examine the decisions players make inside a small request
alongside the changes those decisions leave behind.
